task.goal: Reduce mislabeled samples in a small soil-testing lab during handoffs.
hard_constraints: Two technicians process 40 samples daily with printed labels and one shared spreadsheet; no barcode purchase.
Original samples and identifiers must remain traceable; do not relabel from memory.
Measure wrong labels, handoff time and unresolved mismatches over two weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing intake forms and last month's correction log.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Independent identifier check at each handoff
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make every transfer a two-person comparison against the original intake form. The sender presents one sample and its form; the receiver independently reads the identifier from each before checking the spreadsheet row. Transfer completes only when all three agree. This could reduce errors by replacing assumed agreement with an explicit check against the source record.

Add sender initials, receiver initials, handoff time and mismatch status to the existing spreadsheet. Keep the original sample identifier and intake record unchanged. If identifiers disagree, stop that sample, record the conflicting values and resolve only from documentary evidence. If the evidence is insufficient, leave the sample unresolved and outside processing; never reconstruct its identity from memory.

This requires both technicians to overlap briefly at transfers and intake forms to distinguish samples reliably. No equipment purchase is needed. The main limits are interruption cost, superficial checking and mistakes already shared by both the form and label. Checking cannot establish identity when the source evidence itself is ambiguous. Reversal simply removes the additional handoff check while retaining its audit records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over two weeks, alternate comparable small batches between the current handoff procedure and the independent check. Apply the same brief post-handoff comparison against intake forms to both groups before further processing, correcting or holding discrepancies immediately. Record wrong labels per sample handed off, mismatches caught before acceptance, elapsed handoff time per batch and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Count each discrepancy once and distinguish detected errors from errors that escaped acceptance. Use last month's correction log to choose relevant error categories, not as a directly comparable error rate. The smallest falsifying check is whether checked batches show fewer errors escaping acceptance; equal or worse performance with consistently longer transfers would weaken the case. With about 400 samples, rare errors may leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep samples and source paperwork together in fixed positions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent identity swaps by reducing separation and rearrangement. Use existing bench space to give each sample a distinct position, with its intake form immediately beside it and its printed identifier visible. Transfer small groups in the same physical order, moving each sample and its form together. Only one sample at a time may leave its position for work; return it before opening the next position. Record each sample's temporary position in the shared spreadsheet, while keeping its original identifier authoritative.

The mechanism is physical continuity: fewer simultaneously loose samples and forms create fewer opportunities for accidental exchanges. A position is only a handling aid and must never become evidence for assigning an identifier. If a sample is found outside its expected position or its label disagrees with its form, pause it and use existing documentary evidence to investigate. Preserve the original label and record any correction explicitly.

This needs enough existing space to separate a small group safely, and paperwork placement compatible with the lab's contamination controls. Use smaller groups if space is tight; if safe separation is impossible, this alternative is unsuitable. It may slow work that normally processes several open samples simultaneously and will not repair incorrect intake labels. The procedure is reversible by ending fixed-position handling and retaining the movement records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the two weeks, alternate comparable groups between current handling and fixed-position handling, balancing both methods across days and technicians. Before either group's next processing step, compare labels with intake forms using the same inspection. Log wrong labels per sample, handoff duration, discrepancies caught during movement and unresolved mismatches at day end. Note position departures as a process observation, not proof of mislabeling. Review last month's correction log for documented swaps or separated paperwork to assess whether this mechanism addresses a known problem. A small falsifying check is whether fixed-position groups still experience exchanges or show no improvement in label agreement while adding substantial time. If no errors occur in either group, report feasibility and timing only; error reduction remains uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Receiver-controlled transfer with explicit custody states
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace informal drop-offs with a receiver-controlled queue. In the shared spreadsheet, give each original sample identifier one current custodian and one state: processing, ready for transfer, accepted or mismatch hold. The sender finishes the relevant row and marks the sample ready while retaining custody. The receiver takes one ready sample at a time, checks its printed identifier against its intake form and spreadsheet row, then records acceptance and becomes its custodian. Until acceptance, responsibility remains with the sender.

This changes the handoff from an ambiguous event into a recorded state transition. It could reduce labels being applied or spreadsheet entries being edited against the wrong sample when both technicians assume the other has taken responsibility. Only the current custodian handles that sample's labeling or identity-related spreadsheet edits. Coordinate edits to the single shared sheet sequentially; this does not require additional software.

Keep original identifiers and source records intact. Record discrepancies before any documented correction, and retain unresolved samples in mismatch hold without guessing identity. This assumes technicians can access the shared sheet at transfer points and consistently update it. It can create a queue, does not prevent every physical swap and cannot resolve ambiguous intake evidence. Reversal restores the previous handoff convention while preserving the added custody history.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate comparable batches between current handoffs and receiver-controlled transfers. For both methods, perform the same label-to-intake inspection immediately after handoff and before further processing. Record wrong labels per sample, elapsed time from ready-for-transfer to acceptance, active handoff time and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Record missing or contradictory custody entries separately. Use the correction log to identify documented ownership or spreadsheet-update problems that this procedure might address. The smallest falsifying check is whether completed custody records coexist with the same label-error frequency and longer transfer delays; that would suggest unclear ownership is not the main cause. A quiet two-week period can establish practicality, but cannot establish a reliable reduction in rare errors.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Print labels only when the destination sample is ready
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace advance printing of loose label batches with printing for one sample at the moment its container or derived portion needs a label. Finish applying that sample's labels before requesting another sample's labels. Remove obsolete or duplicate loose labels from the working area and record discarded reprints. The mechanism is eliminating surplus labels that can migrate to another sample during a handoff.

Use the existing printer and spreadsheet. Select the identifier from the intake record, print only the labels needed for the current operation, and retain the original container label and intake form. For derived portions, record their relationship to the original identifier in the spreadsheet. If printing is interrupted or a label's intended destination becomes uncertain, discard the unused label and restart from documentary evidence. Never assign a loose label based on memory.

This assumes the existing printer can economically print individual labels or small sets. Check that capability before adopting the procedure; a printer requiring full sheets may make it impractical. It also assumes labels can be applied safely at the relevant work step. It will not fix incorrect intake records or an incorrect identifier selected for printing. Reversal restores batch printing while keeping the trial records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First inspect last month's correction log for documented loose-label swaps, duplicate labels or reprint confusion. Then alternate comparable batches between current printing and printing on demand over two weeks, distributing both methods across technicians and days. Inspect both groups against intake forms immediately after handoff and before further processing, holding discrepancies immediately.

Record wrong labels per sample, active handoff time, total labeling time, discarded labels and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Distinguish errors intercepted before handoff from errors found afterward. The smallest practical check is one comparable batch under each method: can the existing printer support the workflow without creating a backlog? Continued loose-label mix-ups or increased errors would challenge the mechanism. No errors in either group would establish feasibility, not prove error reduction.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Carry identifiers forward electronically instead of retyping them
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the original intake identifier as a protected source value in the shared spreadsheet. Where identifiers are currently retyped for handoff lists or printed labels, replace retyping with a direct cell reference, copy from the verified source cell, or an existing spreadsheet print template. Display the full identifier without truncation. The mechanism is removing repeated transcription opportunities, especially digit reversals and omitted characters.

For the trial, retain the original spreadsheet and create a clearly marked working copy using the same software. Check each source identifier against its intake form before protecting that column. Keep a separate append-only correction table containing the original value, corrected value, documentary basis, date and technician initials. Protection prevents accidental edits; it does not establish that an identifier is correct. Coordinate edits sequentially between the two technicians.

This requires the spreadsheet's existing features to support references and protection, and the existing printing method to accept spreadsheet values. If label generation necessarily requires manual re-entry, the intervention has less reach. Selecting the wrong source row remains possible, and a wrong source identifier can propagate consistently. Preserve original labels and forms; hold any disagreement until documentary evidence supports resolution. Reversal means returning to the original workbook while retaining the trial and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Inspect the correction log first to determine whether transcription errors are documented. Over two weeks, alternate comparable batches between existing entry practices and electronic carry-forward. Use the same post-handoff comparison with intake forms for both groups before processing continues.

Record wrong labels per sample, handoff duration, unresolved mismatches at day end, and whether each discrepancy concerns transcription, wrong-row selection or ambiguous source evidence. Include setup time separately. The smallest falsifying inspection is to follow several identifiers from intake through spreadsheet to printed label: any required retyping reveals an incomplete implementation. If transcription errors persist or wrong-row errors offset their reduction, the procedure needs revision. With roughly 400 samples and potentially rare errors, report uncertainty rather than treating zero observed errors as proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Separate samples with easily confused identifiers in the work sequence
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce confusion by keeping samples with similar identifiers out of consecutive handoffs. At the start of each day, inspect the intake list for identifiers that differ by one character, reverse adjacent digits, or share a long prefix. Use last month's correction log to prioritize confusion patterns actually documented. Sequence otherwise interchangeable work so these samples are separated by clearly different identifiers, and flag the full identifiers in the shared spreadsheet.

The mechanism is reducing interference between similar names during selection and transfer. Identifiers, printed labels and intake forms remain unchanged; the sequence supplies no evidence of identity. Any disagreement must still be recorded and investigated from original documentation, with unresolved samples held out of processing. Never infer a sample's identifier from its expected place in the sequence.

Implementation needs only a short daily scheduling pass and an added spreadsheet flag. It assumes some samples have confusable identifiers and that processing order can change without violating holding times, analytical requirements or contamination controls. Where order is constrained, apply separation only within interchangeable groups. If identifiers are already distinctive, this procedure has little likely benefit. Reversal simply restores the usual sequence while retaining trial records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
Over two weeks, alternate comparable half-day blocks between usual ordering and similarity-separated ordering, distributing both across technicians and days. Apply the same post-handoff inspection against intake forms in both conditions before further processing. Record wrong labels per sample handed off, handoff time, scheduling time separately, and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Retain the conflicting values so suspected lookalike errors can be distinguished from other errors.

The smallest practical check is one day's intake: can the technicians identify confusable pairs and separate them without delaying required work? If similar identifiers remain adjacent despite resequencing, implementation has failed. If separation is achieved but relevant errors persist at the same frequency with added delay, the proposed mechanism is weakened. Few or no errors over roughly 400 samples would leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep spreadsheet records intact during sorting and filtering
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent a spreadsheet operation from separating identifiers from the sample information beside them. Inspect the shared workbook for separately sortable columns, merged cells, blank rows inside the sample list, or handoff lists created by copying individual columns. Convert the active sample range into one contiguous table using existing spreadsheet features, with one complete record per row. Sort and filter through that table only; generate any handoff printout from complete rows.

The mechanism is preserving the relationship between each identifier and its associated data. A partial-column sort can make a correct identifier appear beside another sample's information, potentially causing subsequent label selection errors. This intervention addresses that structural failure rather than relying on technicians to notice each displaced value.

Before the trial, retain a dated workbook copy and verify the table's identifier-to-intake relationships. Keep original forms and container labels intact. Record corrections separately with old value, new value, documentary basis and technician initials; hold ambiguous samples without guessing. Coordinate edits sequentially in the single shared spreadsheet.

This requires table or equivalent whole-range sorting support in the existing software. It assumes spreadsheet rearrangement contributes to handoff errors; inspect the correction log and current workflow before investing effort. It cannot prevent physical sample swaps or an incorrect initial entry. Reversal restores the former layout after reconciling trial records, without discarding the audit history.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First use a disposable copy of several existing records to compare the current sorting workflow with the contiguous-table workflow. Inspect whether every identifier retains all its associated fields after ordinary sorts and filters. Do not introduce deliberate errors into the live workbook. If the current workflow already guarantees intact rows, this alternative has little additional value.

For the two-week live trial, use the verified table and apply the same intake-based inspection after each handoff. Record wrong labels per sample, elapsed handoff time and unresolved mismatches at each day's end; log setup time separately. Compare daily counts cautiously with the correction log, acknowledging differences in detection and workload. Any displaced identifier-to-data relationship after a permitted table operation falsifies the structural safeguard. Zero observed errors supports feasibility but cannot establish a reduction without a comparable baseline.

EXPAND.title: Retain the original label through handoffs
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove routine replacement labels at transfers wherever the existing label remains readable and suitable for the next step. This targets errors introduced by recreating an identifier that the sample already carries.

Before starting, the two technicians use intake forms and last month's correction log to identify which steps currently replace or duplicate labels and why. For eligible samples, keep the original printed label attached and pass the original intake form with the sample. Record stage changes in the existing spreadsheet under its original identifier. Do not create a fresh label merely to indicate a new processing stage.

If a label is damaged, a new container is required, or an established laboratory requirement mandates another label, use the existing documented replacement procedure. Preserve the old label or its recorded contents and the link between containers. If identity cannot be established from records, hold the sample unresolved; never reconstruct it from memory.

The mechanism is elimination of an error-producing operation. Unlike the prior independent-check route, it reduces opportunities to introduce wrong labels before checking becomes necessary. It requires no purchase and is reversible by restoring routine label production while retaining the trial records. Its suitability is uncertain until current labeling practices are inspected: if handoffs already retain original labels, this route offers little benefit. Label durability and readability are the principal limits.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician A owns a two-week trial covering eligible samples, with both technicians processing them. Alternate comparable batches between retaining original labels and routine relabeling with the prior independent handoff check. Give both groups the same final comparison against intake forms before further processing.

Record wrong labels per sample, active handoff time, label preparation time, unreadable labels and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Preserve discrepancy details before correction. Stop the trial method for any processing condition that makes retained labels unreadable or violates a required labeling step; hold affected samples until documentary resolution. The smallest useful inspection is one matched pair of batches: fewer label operations without better accuracy or lower total work would weaken the case. Two weeks without errors establishes feasibility, not a reliable reduction.

EXPAND.title: Allow only one sample's labels in each print job
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent labels from different samples becoming mixed between printing and application. Print labels for one sample at a time, apply them to that sample's required containers, and reconcile the job before printing for another sample. This changes label production rather than the physical arrangement of samples or the acceptance check.

At preparation, open the sample's existing spreadsheet record and compare its identifier with the original intake form. Determine the required number of labels. Print only that identifier, apply the labels while the original sample and form are present, and record the printed, applied and discarded counts in the shared spreadsheet. Both technicians use a single printing sequence so jobs cannot interleave. Remove unused labels from circulation after recording their disposal; preserve original sample labels and identifiers.

If a job contains an unexpected identifier, quantity or stale output, suspend application and reconcile the entire job against documentary records. Hold any container whose identity is uncertain. An apparently correct count does not establish identity.

This requires the existing printer to support single-sample jobs without purchasing equipment. It may consume more paper or printer time, and it cannot prevent selecting the wrong source record. The correction log can indicate whether mixed labels or surplus labels have occurred, but cannot establish that this is the dominant cause. Compared with the prior independent handoff check, this route prevents a specific upstream mix-up that checking might miss or discover only after application. Reversal restores batch printing while preserving the reconciliation history.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician B owns a two-week comparison of matched small batches: isolated print jobs versus existing batch printing with the prior independent handoff check. Use the same post-handoff label-to-intake inspection in both arms.

Measure wrong labels per sample, handoff time, total printing/application time, discarded labels and daily unresolved mismatches. Stop isolated printing if jobs cannot be kept separate or label reconciliation fails; quarantine affected material for documentary investigation. One pair of ordinary batches can expose impractical printer overhead. If accuracy is no better and total work or waste rises, the route has not shown an advantage. Report uncertainty if label errors are too rare to distinguish the methods.

EXPAND.title: Carry the identifier forward within one spreadsheet record
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove repeated typing of sample identifiers during stage updates. Establish one spreadsheet row per original sample and enter subsequent processing results and handoff information in that row, using additional stage columns where necessary. The original identifier is entered once from the intake form and then retained as text, including leading zeros.

Before the trial, the technicians reconcile active rows against intake forms and flag duplicate or ambiguous identifiers. Preserve the original sheet as a dated worksheet within the same workbook. Protect the identifier column if the existing spreadsheet supports it; otherwise clearly mark it as requiring a documented correction. At each stage, locate the existing record using the full printed identifier, confirm the matching intake form, and update only that row. Keep the identifier visible during entry, and sort complete rows only.

This targets transcription errors and broken links between separate stage records. It differs from receiver-controlled custody: it changes how identity data is carried forward, rather than who owns a transfer. It needs only the current spreadsheet and modest setup time. It assumes the workflow can fit within a single record per sample; if repeated results require extra rows, each must retain an explicit documentary link to the original record.

A protected identifier can still belong to the wrong selected row. Duplicate identifiers, ambiguous forms or uncertain row selection therefore trigger a hold, not a guessed assignment. Corrections must preserve the original value, replacement value, evidence and technician initials. Reversal restores the saved layout while retaining trial records.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician A owns a two-week pilot on comparable batches, comparing single-record updates with the current spreadsheet workflow plus the prior independent handoff check. Apply the same final intake-based inspection to both groups.

Measure wrong physical labels and wrong spreadsheet associations separately, alongside handoff time, spreadsheet entry time and daily unresolved mismatches. Stop the pilot if a sort separates identifiers from results or if the layout obscures required processing records; reconcile affected rows before continuing. Inspect one completed batch end to end for missing results and wrong-row entries. No reduction in errors, coupled with slower entry or more wrong-row associations, would defeat the proposed benefit. Historical corrections help classify errors but are not a comparable control.

EXPAND.title: Assign each sample's full processing sequence to one technician
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove an avoidable handoff by assigning each technician a set of samples to process from intake preparation through completion. Divide the day's 40 samples according to expected workload and required competence. Each technician keeps responsibility for labeling, spreadsheet entries and processing of their assigned samples, using existing intake forms and printed identifiers.

Before starting, identify steps that truly require the other technician, shared equipment or independent review. Equipment can remain shared without transferring sample responsibility: the assigned technician performs the step when it becomes available. Keep any required independent review. For unavoidable transfers, use the prior independent identifier check and document the exception. Do not create an informal workaround if a technician lacks competence or availability.

The mechanism is fewer transfers and fewer changes of handling context. It differs from the prior custody-state route, which records and controls transfers while retaining them. It requires both technicians to be qualified for the relevant sequence and sufficient scheduling flexibility. It could create queues, reduce specialization benefits or let one technician's initial mistake persist, so completion review must still compare the original label, intake form and spreadsheet record.

Preserve original identifiers throughout. Investigate discrepancies from documentary evidence, record corrections and hold unresolved samples. The procedure is reversible by returning to stage-based work allocation. If most transfers are mandatory, this route has little scope; the first inspection should establish how many can actually be eliminated.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician B owns a two-week trial alternating comparable batches between full-sequence assignment and stage-based work with the prior independent handoff check. Balance assignments across technicians and use the same completion inspection for both methods.

Record wrong labels per sample, total handoff time per batch, time per remaining handoff, daily unresolved mismatches, completion time and unfinished samples. Stop full-sequence assignment for a batch if it causes a required processing deadline to be missed or requires work beyond a technician's competence; use a documented checked transfer instead. A matched day's batches can test whether fewer handoffs improve accuracy or merely shift work into queues. Equal accuracy with worse completion performance would weaken the proposal. Rare errors may leave the two-week result inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Make independent handoff checks restartable after interruption
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the independent identifier-check route: retain the comparison of sample label, original intake form and spreadsheet, but make acceptance an explicit transaction. The sender retains responsibility until the receiver finishes checking and records acceptance. The receiver reads the identifiers directly before hearing the sender's expected value. If interrupted before acceptance, the sender keeps the sample and form together; both restart the comparison from the beginning. An unfinished check never counts as acceptance.

This closes a consequential interruption gap in the original procedure while preserving its main mechanism: checking against documentary evidence. Either technician may send or receive. Use the existing spreadsheet for sender, receiver, acceptance time and mismatch status. Preserve original labels and record conflicting values and any evidence-backed correction. Hold unresolved samples outside processing; never assign identity from memory.

This needs brief overlap between technicians and accessible, sufficiently clear intake records. When overlap is unavailable, the sender retains custody and the transfer waits. Ambiguous source records trigger a hold. Compared with an informal or partially completed check, restarting could prevent unchecked transfers, but adds waiting and repeated work. It cannot detect an incorrect identity already shared by all records. Rollback removes the acceptance procedure while retaining its audit history.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician A coordinates a two-week trial, with both technicians applying the procedure to the day's 40 samples. First inspect one small batch and rehearse an interruption before acceptance using clearly identified samples; confirm that custody remains explicit and the comparison restarts. Stop further transfers under the trial if either technician cannot establish who holds responsibility; reconcile the affected sample against records before resuming.

Measure wrong labels per sample, discrepancies caught before acceptance, elapsed handoff time including waiting, active checking time and unresolved mismatches at each day's end. Preserve discrepancy details before correction and count each event once. Use last month's correction log to classify errors, not to claim a comparable historical rate. Inspect whether interrupted transfers escape acceptance without a complete check. Review after two days and at two weeks: persistent waiting that prevents daily processing, or repeated incomplete acceptance records, calls for rollback. A small or zero error count cannot establish reliable error reduction.

EXPAND.title: Transfer fixed-position groups with an explicit partial-transfer rule
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the fixed-position route by defining what happens when a group transfer stops halfway. Retain distinct sample positions, adjacent intake forms, visible printed identifiers and one-sample-at-a-time work. Add this rule: transfer each sample and its form as one unit, and record receiver acceptance before moving the next unit. The sender remains responsible for every unaccepted sample. Following an interruption, resume from the acceptance record only after checking the next sample against its original intake form; position alone never establishes identity.

This preserves the physical-continuity mechanism while preventing a partly moved group from becoming an ambiguous shared pile. Both technicians own their respective sending and receiving actions. Use existing bench space and the shared spreadsheet; retain temporary position records and add acceptance initials. If either technician cannot reconcile the physical group with accepted and unaccepted records, pause that group and inspect every affected sample against documentary evidence. Preserve original identifiers, document corrections and hold unresolved material.

This assumes safe space for separated samples and paperwork. Reduce group size when space is limited; if even one unit cannot be kept safely distinct, use direct checked transfers without the position arrangement. Compared with the original group movement, sequential acceptance adds spreadsheet work but may contain interruption-related mix-ups. It will not repair an incorrect intake identity. Rollback ends fixed-position handling while preserving trial and correction records.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician B coordinates two weeks of comparable small batches alternating between the original fixed-position procedure and this partial-transfer rule. Apply the same label-to-intake inspection after handoff and before processing in both groups. Start with one small batch and a deliberate pause between completed unit transfers, without obscuring or exchanging identifiers.

Measure wrong labels per sample, handoff time including interruption recovery, active transfer time and daily unresolved mismatches. Separately record ambiguous custody and time spent reconciling partial groups. Stop the upgraded method for a group if safe separation fails or acceptance records cannot be reconciled; hold affected samples for documentary investigation and revert subsequent groups to direct checked transfers.

Use the correction log to identify relevant separation or interruption incidents. The upgrade earns its additional entry burden only if partial transfers remain easier to reconstruct or fewer errors escape acceptance. If both methods have no errors, report timing and recoverability rather than claiming improved accuracy.

EXPAND.title: Separate confusing identifiers in the processing sequence
EXPAND.proposal:
Use identifier similarity to schedule work so easily confused samples are not handled consecutively. This changes the sequence of exposure to lookalike identifiers, rather than adding another handoff check, changing custody or recreating labels.

At the existing daily intake review, the two technicians inspect the day's identifiers and use last month's correction log to identify documented confusion patterns, such as transposed digits or identifiers differing only at the end. Mark potentially confusing pairs in the shared spreadsheet and place them in separate processing groups, with unrelated samples between them where practical. Preserve every original printed label and intake record. Change processing order only where existing laboratory timing and handling requirements permit; sequence is never evidence of identity.

Technician A prepares the order and Technician B checks that it is operationally feasible. If a priority change brings a marked pair into the same group, defer one where allowed; otherwise process the two separately with a direct label-to-intake comparison at each transfer. Unclear identities remain on hold for documentary resolution, with corrections recorded rather than reconstructed from memory.

The hypothesis is that reducing immediate exposure to similar identifiers reduces selection and transcription confusion. It requires only a short daily review and spreadsheet annotations, but its value is uncertain until the log and current identifiers show relevant patterns. Compared with ordinary ordering, it adds planning and may disrupt efficient batching. If mandatory processing order prevents separation, this route has little scope. Rollback restores normal sequencing and retains the annotations.
EXPAND.experiment:
Technician A owns a two-week trial. First inspect the correction log and one day's identifiers; proceed only if at least one plausible confusing pair can be separated without compromising required processing order. For eligible groups, alternate ordinary ordering and separated ordering across comparable workloads, retaining existing handoff checks and using the same post-handoff intake comparison in both conditions.

Measure wrong labels per sample, handoff time, daily unresolved mismatches, planning time and processing delays. Record whether errors involve identifiers marked as confusing. Stop reordering any group when it threatens a required processing time or creates an uncertain sample-to-record association; restore feasible order and investigate affected material from records.

The smallest inspection is one day's planned and actual sequence: verify that marked pairs were separated and quantify the extra planning and waiting. If no relevant pairs exist, discontinue the route. If errors are rare over two weeks, report feasibility and cost without claiming that sequencing reduced mislabeling.
